Un tren que frena sin rozar nada: A train that brakes without touching anything
no hay zapatas ni pastillas: ni se gasta: no shoes or pads: they do not wear out, the wheels do not heat up, and they do not depend on the track being wet.
Al final de una montaña rusa el vagón en: At the end of a roller coaster the car enters at 70 km/h a zone with large magnets on both sides of the track and stops smoothly, without a squeal. There are no brake shoes rubbing: under the car hangs only a metal fin, which passes between the magnets without touching them.\n\nSo who brakes? The motion itself. Magnetic brakes use a consequence of Faraday's law: **a metal moving in a magnetic field slows down by itself**. And the same principle, in reverse, makes levitation trains float.

The magnets are above and below, facing each other, and between the two there is a zone with an almost uniform field $B$ that **comes out of the screen** (the dots ⊙). Outside that zone the field is almost zero.\n\nThe fin, made of copper or aluminium, is a good conductor and moves at speed $v$: it goes in on one side of the field zone and out the other. One part of it is always inside the field, and the part entering or leaving is the one that matters.

Dentro del campo, el flujo que atraviesa:
Inside the field, the flux through any circuit drawn on the fin changes as it enters or leaves the zone. For a strip of width $L$ moving at speed $v$, Faraday's law gives the motional emf:

$ε = −{dΦ}/{dt} = B L v$

With $B$ = 1 T, $L$ = 0.5 m and $v$ = 20 m/s, we get $ε$ = **${n(datos.eps, 0)} V**. It is the same as the emf of a bar sliding on rails: no battery or cable is needed, the motion creates it.
frena el vagón a ${V0} m/s, con una corr: brakes the car at ${V0} m/s, with a current of ${n(datos.I / 1000, 0)} kA through the fin.
Como la aleta es un metal macizo, esa fe:
Since the fin is solid metal, that emf does not go nowhere: it makes closed currents circulate, the eddy currents, with a swirl on each side of the field zone. Their equivalent resistance is very small (≈ 0.5 mΩ), so $I = ε/R = ${n(datos.eps, 0)}/0.0005$ = **${miles(datos.I)} A**.

A current in a field feels the force $F = I L B$. And, by Lenz's law, it has the direction that opposes the cause: it brakes. Substituting $I$:

$F = I L B = {B^2 L^2 v}/R = K v$ = **${miles(datos.F)} N**

The force is proportional to the speed, with $K = B^2 L^2 / R$ = ${miles(K)} N·s/m. Move the slider to see it.
Frena mucho al principio y se apaga: It brakes strongly at first and dies away
es lo que tarda en bajar a un 37 % la ve: is how long it takes the speed of a ${miles(MASA)} kg car to drop to 37 %; at ${n(5, 0)} s it goes at ${n(datos.v5, 1)} m/s.
Como $F = K v$, la deceleración es $a =: Since $F = K v$, the deceleration is $a = F/m$ = ${n(datos.a, 1)} m/s² (half a g) at 20 m/s, but **it falls as the car slows**: at 5 m/s it is already four times smaller. The equation $m dv/dt = −K v$ gives an exponential decay: $v(t) = v_0 e^{−t/τ}$, with $τ = m/K$ = **${n(TAU, 0)} s** The kinetic energy, ${n(datos.Ec / 1000, 0)} kJ, is turned into heat in the fin by the Joule effect (at the start, $P = ε I$ = ${n(datos.P / 1000, 0)} kW). That is why the magnetic brake never stops completely: it is perfect for taking off speed smoothly, but in the end friction brakes are needed to hold the car at rest.
El tren de levitación: el mismo principi: The levitation train: the same principle
es el récord de velocidad de un tren: el: is the speed record for a train: the Japanese SCMaglev, in 2015. It lifts off its wheels at around 150 km/h.
Un tren de levitación electrodinámico ll: An electrodynamic levitation train carries powerful superconducting magnets. In the track there are coils closed on themselves. When the train passes, the magnet changes the flux in each coil: by Faraday currents are induced, and by Lenz those currents create a field that **repels** the magnet and holds it up. With the train's magnets, the coil behaves like a brake that, instead of braking, **lifts**.\n\nIf the train is at rest there is no changing flux, no currents, no force: it rests on wheels. With a simple model (the coil with $R$ and $L$), the fraction of the weight supported by levitation is $v^2/(v^2 + v_c^2)$, with $v_c$ = ${VC} m/s: at 30 m/s it is half, and at 140 m/s (500 km/h) it is already ${n(100 * levita(140), 0)} %.
